- If sentiment shows strong bullish (≥0.67) or bearish (≤-0.33) momentum in recent days, model should adjust forecast directionally — avoid ignoring sentiment drift.
- When model forecasts a sharp spike (e.g., >+3% from recent high), reduce subsequent forecast values to avoid overshoot; true outcomes often correct downward within 3–5 days.
- If recent history shows mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of declining prices), model should not assume continuation; expect reversal or consolidation.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome deviates >10% from forecast mean, check sentiment history for “reversal” signals (e.g., 2+ consecutive negative sentiment) — model may be overconfident.
- If sentiment history includes 1–2 strong bearish signals (e.g., 1.00 or -1.00) within last 5 days, reduce forecast mean by 2–5% to account for potential downward pressure.
- Avoid forecasting “flat” or “neutral” when sentiment shows clear direction — even if price is stable, sentiment can trigger sudden moves.
- If model forecasts a 30-day trend that contradicts recent 7-day average (e.g., forecast rising while 7-day avg is falling), flag for correction — true outcomes often revert to shorter-term mean.
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, if sentiment is neutral or mixed (0.00–0.33), model should not assume strong trend — true outcomes often show volatility or mean reversion within 10–15 days.
